title: Big-O
summary: Time complexity vs Space complexity, asymptotic analysis, O(1), O(log N), O(N), O(N log N), O(N^2), O(2^N).

explanation.overview: Big-O notation describes the worst-case limiting behavior of an algorithm's execution time or memory space usage as input size $N$ grows.

sections.heading: Common Time Complexities (Fast to Slow)
sections.content:
1. $O(1)$ **Constant**: Array index access, Hash Map lookup.
2. $O(\log N)$ **Logarithmic**: Binary Search, Balanced BST lookup.
3. $O(N)$ **Linear**: Single loop search across array.
4. $O(N \log N)$ **Linearithmic**: Efficient sorting (Merge Sort, QuickSort).
5. $O(N^2)$ **Quadratic**: Nested loops (Bubble Sort).
6. $O(2^N)$ **Exponential**: Recursive Fibonacci without memoization.
bulletPoints: O(1): Instant execution regardless of input size.
O(log N): Input halved at each step.
O(N): Execution grows linearly with input.

sections.heading: Space Complexity & Auxiliary Memory
sections.content: Space complexity measures extra auxiliary memory allocated by algorithm (recursion stack frames, hash tables, temporary arrays) relative to input $N$.
bulletPoints: In-Place Algorithms: $O(1)$ extra space usage.
Recursion Stack: Recursive calls consume $O(H)$ stack space matching call tree depth.

keyTakeaways: Big-O measures worst-case asymptotic upper bound growth.
Hierarchy: $O(1) < O(\log N) < O(N) < O(N \log N) < O(N^2) < O(2^N)$.
Account for both Time complexity and Space complexity.

mcqs.explanation: Binary Search halves search space at each iteration step, yielding $O(\log N)$ logarithmic time.

options: O(1) < O(log N) < O(N) < O(N log N) < O(N^2)
mcqs.explanation: Correct growth hierarchy is $O(1) < O(\log N) < O(N) < O(N \log N) < O(N^2)$.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of 2 nested loops running $N$ iterations each `for i in N: for j in N:`?
mcqs.explanation: Nested loops running $N$ times each perform $N \times N = N^2$ operations ($O(N^2)$).

mcqs.question: What does Space Complexity measure in algorithm analysis?
options: Auxiliary memory allocated by algorithm as input size N increases
mcqs.explanation: Space complexity quantifies additional RAM allocated during execution.

title: Arrays
summary: Contiguous memory layout, indexed access O(1), search O(N), insertion/deletion O(N), and dynamic arrays.

explanation.overview: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory locations, enabling instant $O(1)$ random access by index.

sections.heading: Time Complexities of Array Operations
sections.content:
- **Access by Index**: $O(1)$ (Memory address offset = `base + index * element_size`).
- **Search**: $O(N)$ (Un-sorted array linear scan).
- **Insertion / Deletion at End**: $O(1)$ amortized.
- **Insertion / Deletion at Start/Middle**: $O(N)$ (Requires shifting subsequent elements in memory).
bulletPoints: Access: $O(1)$ constant time.
Insert at Start: $O(N)$ linear time due to memory shifting.
Delete at End: $O(1)$ constant time.

sections.heading: Dynamic Arrays (ArrayList / Vector / JS Array)
sections.content: Dynamic arrays automatically resize capacity when full (doubling array capacity). Reallocating memory and copying elements yields $O(1)$ amortized insertion cost.
bulletPoints: Doubling Strategy: Capacity doubles when full.
Amortized $O(1)$: Occasional $O(N)$ resize cost averaged over $N$ pushes.

keyTakeaways: Array index access is $O(1)$ constant time.
Inserting or deleting elements at start/middle costs $O(N)$ due to shifting.
Dynamic array `push` has $O(1)$ amortized time complexity.

options: All existing N elements must be shifted 1 position right in contiguous memory
mcqs.explanation: Inserting at start requires shifting all subsequent elements right in memory.

mcqs.question: What is amortized time complexity of appending an element to end of a dynamic array `arr.push()`?
mcqs.explanation: Array capacity doubling makes append operations run in $O(1)$ amortized time.

mcqs.explanation: Contiguous memory layout allows calculating target memory address via arithmetic offset.

mcqs.question: What is worst-case time complexity of linear search on an un-sorted array of N elements?
mcqs.explanation: Linear search checks every element in worst case, running in $O(N)$ time.

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of creating a 2D matrix array of dimensions $N \times N$?
mcqs.explanation: An $N \times N$ 2D matrix allocates $N^2$ memory cells ($O(N^2)$ space).

title: Strings
summary: String immutability, character encoding (ASCII/Unicode), string manipulation, and string building optimization.

explanation.overview: Strings are sequences of characters. In JavaScript, Python, and Java, strings are immutable primitive values.

sections.heading: String Immutability Pitfall
sections.content: In immutable string languages, concatenating strings inside a loop (`str += char`) creates a fresh string object on every iteration, leading to an accidental $O(N^2)$ time complexity!
bulletPoints: String Immutability: Modifying string creates new string copy.
Loop Concatenation Pitfall: `str += char` inside $N$-length loop costs $O(N^2)$ time.
Array Join Solution: Push chars to array and execute `arr.join('')` ($O(N)$ time).

sections.heading: ASCII vs Unicode Encoding
sections.content: ASCII uses 7/8 bits per character (128 chars). Unicode (UTF-8 / UTF-16) uses variable 1-4 bytes to represent global language scripts and emojis.
bulletPoints: ASCII: 256 standard character set.
UTF-8: Variable length encoding (1 to 4 bytes per character).

keyTakeaways: Strings are immutable in JS/Python/Java.
Avoid string concatenation in loops; collect in array and `join('')` ($O(N)$).
Unicode characters can consume multiple byte code points.

codeExamples.description: Array join pattern vs string concatenation loop.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of appending $N$ characters one-by-one to a string inside a loop `str += char` in immutable string languages (JS/Java)?
mcqs.explanation: Because strings are immutable, copying strings of length $1, 2, ..., N$ sums to $O(N^2)$ total operations.

mcqs.question: How should string building inside loops be optimized in JavaScript for $O(N)$ efficiency?
options: Push character substrings to an array and call `arr.join('')`
mcqs.explanation: Collecting elements in array and joining once allocates memory in single linear $O(N)$ pass.

mcqs.question: What does 'String Immutability' mean?
options: Once created, string character content in memory cannot be modified in-place; alterations create new string instances
mcqs.explanation: Immutability means existing string objects in memory cannot be mutated.

mcqs.explanation: Two pointers checking characters from ends run in linear $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ constant space.

mcqs.question: How many bytes does a standard ASCII character consume in memory?
mcqs.explanation: Standard ASCII characters consume exactly 1 byte (8 bits) of storage.

title: Hash maps
summary: Key-value pair lookups, hash function, collision resolution (Chaining vs Open Addressing), O(1) average lookup.

explanation.overview: Hash Maps (Map / Dictionary) store key-value pairs, providing average $O(1)$ constant time for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations.

sections.heading: Hash Function & Collision Resolution
sections.content:
A **Hash Function** maps key string/object to integer array index. When two keys produce identical bucket indexes (Collision), Hash Maps use:
- **Separate Chaining**: Bucket contains linked list or red-black tree of colliding key-value pairs.
- **Open Addressing**: Probes alternative array slots (Linear Probing / Quadratic Probing).
bulletPoints: Hash Function: Converts key into array index.
Separate Chaining: Linked list at array bucket index.
Worst-case O(N): High collision rate degrades lookup to $O(N)$.

sections.heading: Two-Sum Problem Pattern
sections.content: Hash Maps trade $O(N)$ space complexity to optimize nested loop searches ($O(N^2)$) down to single pass $O(N)$ linear time.
bulletPoints: Space-Time Tradeoff: Store visited elements in Map to achieve $O(1)$ lookups.

keyTakeaways: Hash Maps offer average $O(1)$ lookup, insert, and delete operations.
Collisions are resolved via Separate Chaining or Open Addressing.
Use Hash Maps for $O(N)$ time solutions to search/lookup problems.

codeExamples.description: Solving Two-Sum in O(N) time with Map.

mcqs.question: What is AVERAGE time complexity of key lookup `map.get(key)` in a Hash Map?
mcqs.explanation: Hash function array bucket mapping executes in average $O(1)$ constant time.

mcqs.question: What is WORST-CASE time complexity of Hash Map lookup if all inserted keys collide into same single bucket index?
mcqs.explanation: If all keys collide into single bucket chain, searching linked list takes $O(N)$ linear time.

mcqs.question: What is 'Separate Chaining' collision resolution mechanism?
options: Storing colliding key-value pairs in a linked list or tree at array bucket index
mcqs.explanation: Separate Chaining stores colliding key-value elements in linked list/tree at bucket index.

mcqs.question: How does using a Hash Map improve Two-Sum problem from naive brute-force $O(N^2)$ to optimal solution?
options: Reduces complement lookup time from $O(N)$ linear search to $O(1)$ Map lookup, achieving $O(N)$ total time
mcqs.explanation: Hash Map enables $O(1)$ complement lookups, reducing overall time to $O(N)$.

mcqs.question: What happens when Hash Map Load Factor (ratio of items to bucket array size) exceeds threshold (e.g. 0.75)?
options: Hash Map automatically rehashes: doubles internal array capacity and re-distributes keys
mcqs.explanation: Exceeding load factor threshold triggers rehashing to expand bucket array and maintain $O(1)$ speeds.

title: Sets
summary: Unique element collections, O(1) add/has/delete, deduplication, and set operations.

explanation.overview: A Set is a data structure that stores unique values without duplicates, offering average $O(1)$ lookup, insertion, and deletion times.

sections.heading: Set Operations & Deduplication
sections.content:
- `add(val)`: Adds unique value ($O(1)$).
- `has(val)`: Checks existence ($O(1)$).
- `delete(val)`: Removes value ($O(1)$).
- Array Deduplication: `Array.from(new Set(arr))` removes duplicate items in linear $O(N)$ time.
bulletPoints: Uniqueness: Automatically discards duplicate insertions.
Fast Existence Check: `set.has(val)` is $O(1)$ vs `arr.includes(val)` ($O(N)$).

sections.heading: Set vs Array Existence Checking
sections.content: Replacing `array.includes(x)` inside a loop ($O(N)$) with `set.has(x)` ($O(1)$) optimizes time complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$.
bulletPoints: Array Includes: $O(N)$ linear scan.
Set Has: $O(1)$ instant hash lookup.

keyTakeaways: Sets store unique elements only.
`set.has(val)` runs in $O(1)$ constant time.
Deduplicate arrays efficiently using `[...new Set(arr)]`.

codeExamples.description: Removing duplicates and instant set existence checking.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of `set.has(value)` in a Hash-based Set?
mcqs.explanation: Hash Set existence check executes in average $O(1)$ constant time.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of deduplicating an array `[...new Set(arr)]` of N elements?
mcqs.explanation: Constructing Set from N elements processes each item once in $O(N)$ time.

mcqs.question: What happens if you execute `set.add(5)` twice on a JavaScript `Set`?
mcqs.explanation: Sets enforce uniqueness; duplicate insertions are ignored.

mcqs.question: Why is `set.has(x)` inside a loop running N times better than `arr.includes(x)`?
options: `set.has(x)` is $O(1)$ making loop $O(N)$, whereas `arr.includes(x)` is $O(N)$ making loop $O(N^2)$
mcqs.explanation: Using $O(1)$ set lookup inside $N$ loop iteration yields $O(N)$ total time instead of $O(N^2)$.

mcqs.question: Do standard JavaScript `Set` instances maintain insertion order during iteration?
options: Yes, ES6 Set iterates elements in exact insertion order
mcqs.explanation: ES6 `Set` iterates elements in order of insertion.

title: Two pointers
summary: Two Pointer pattern, Left/Right converging pointers, Fast/Slow pointers (Floyd Cycle Detection), and O(N) array processing.

explanation.overview: The Two Pointers pattern uses two pointer indexes to iterate through a data structure simultaneously, optimizing space and time complexity.

sections.heading: 2 Primary Two Pointer Variations
sections.content:
1. **Converging Pointers (Left & Right)**: Pointers start at opposite ends (`left = 0`, `right = N-1`) and move toward center. Used for sorted array Two-Sum, Palindromes, Container With Most Water.
2. **Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd Cycle Detection)**: `slow` moves 1 step; `fast` moves 2 steps. Used to detect Linked List cycles and find middle node.
bulletPoints: Left/Right Converging: Requires sorted array or opposite boundary traversal.
Fast/Slow (Tortoise & Hare): Detects loops/cycles in $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

sections.heading: Space Complexity Advantage
sections.content: Two pointer algorithms operate in-place, achieving $O(1)$ constant space complexity without allocating extra arrays or Hash Maps.
bulletPoints: In-Place: Modifies array or checks conditions in $O(1)$ extra space.

keyTakeaways: Converging pointers (Left/Right) optimize sorted array search problems.
Fast/Slow pointers detect linked list cycles in $O(1)$ space.
Two Pointers pattern achieves $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

options: Array MUST be sorted in ascending/descending order
Must contain even number of items
mcqs.explanation: Converging Two Pointers rely on sorted array order to decide whether to increment `left` or decrement `right`.

options: Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare)
mcqs.explanation: Floyd's Cycle Detection uses Fast and Slow pointers to detect linked list loops.

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of Converging Two Pointers Palindrome check algorithm?

mcqs.explanation: Fast pointer moving double speed reaches list end when Slow pointer arrives at middle node.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of Two Pointers reverse array algorithm?
mcqs.explanation: Swapping elements from both ends inward processes $N/2$ pairs in $O(N)$ linear time.

title: Sliding window
summary: Sliding Window pattern, Fixed window size vs Variable window size, contiguous subarray/substring tracking in O(N).

explanation.overview: The Sliding Window pattern reduces nested loop $O(N^2)$ operations on contiguous subarrays or substrings to linear $O(N)$ time by maintaining a sliding window window boundaries (`left`, `right`).

sections.heading: Fixed vs Variable Sliding Window
sections.content:
1. **Fixed Window**: Window size $K$ is constant (e.g. Max sum of subarray of size $K$). Slide window right by adding incoming element and subtracting outgoing element.
2. **Variable Window**: Window shrinks/expands dynamically based on condition (e.g. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters). Expand `right` pointer; shrink `left` pointer when condition is violated.
bulletPoints: Fixed Window: Constant size $K$. Add `right`, subtract `left`.
Variable Window: Dynamic size based on validity criteria.
Contiguous Subarray: Key pattern indicator.

sections.heading: Time Complexity Gain
sections.content: Instead of recalculating sum/counts for entire subarray on each step ($O(N \times K)$), updating sliding window incrementally costs $O(1)$ per step, yielding $O(N)$ overall time.
bulletPoints: Incremental Update: $O(1)$ window adjustment.
Overall Time: $O(N)$ linear execution.

keyTakeaways: Sliding Window solves contiguous subarray/substring problems in $O(N)$ time.
Fixed Window: Maintain constant window size $K$.
Variable Window: Expand `right`, shrink `left` dynamically based on validity.

mcqs.question: What problem characteristic strongly suggests applying the Sliding Window pattern?
options: Contiguous subarray or substring calculation requirements (e.g. max sum of K consecutive elements)
mcqs.explanation: Contiguous subarray or substring problems are prime candidates for Sliding Window.

mcqs.question: How does Fixed Sliding Window calculate sum of next subarray of size K in $O(1)$ time?
options: Subtracts element exiting left window boundary and adds new element entering right window boundary
mcqs.explanation: Incremental update subtracts outgoing left item and adds incoming right item in $O(1)$ time.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of Variable Sliding Window algorithm for Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters?
options: O(N) linear time (each character is processed at most twice by left and right pointers)
mcqs.explanation: Left and right pointers traverse array at most once, yielding $O(N)$ linear time.

mcqs.question: When should left window boundary `left++` shrink in Variable Sliding Window algorithm?
options: When window state violates problem validity constraint (e.g. contains duplicate character or sum exceeds limit)
mcqs.explanation: Shrink left boundary whenever current window state violates validity criteria.

mcqs.question: What auxiliary space complexity is typically required by Sliding Window with a character frequency map/Set for ASCII strings?
options: O(1) constant space (at most 128/256 unique character keys in Set)
mcqs.explanation: ASCII character sets contain at most 128/256 keys, bounding auxiliary space to $O(1)$.

title: Stack
summary: LIFO structure, PUSH, POP, PEEK, Monotonic Stack pattern, and call stack execution.

explanation.overview: A Stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) data structure where elements are added and removed from the top.

sections.heading: Stack Operations & LIFO Order
sections.content:
All operations at top of stack execute in $O(1)$ constant time:
- `push(item)`: Adds element to top ($O(1)$).
- `pop()`: Removes and returns top element ($O(1)$).
- `peek()` / `top()`: Inspects top element without removing ($O(1)$).
bulletPoints: LIFO: Last item pushed is first item popped.
Use Cases: Function call stack, undo/redo buffers, balanced parentheses matching.

sections.heading: Monotonic Stack Pattern
sections.content: A **Monotonic Stack** maintains elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order. Essential for solving Next Greater Element and Daily Temperatures in $O(N)$ time.
bulletPoints: Monotonic Increasing: Elements ordered from smallest to largest.
Next Greater Element: $O(N)$ solution instead of $O(N^2)$ brute force.

keyTakeaways: Stack is LIFO (Last-In, First-Out).
`push`, `pop`, `peek` execute in $O(1)$ constant time.
Monotonic Stack pattern solves Next Greater Element in $O(N)$ time.

mcqs.explanation: Stacks follow LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) operation ordering.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of `push()`, `pop()`, and `peek()` stack operations?
mcqs.explanation: Top-of-stack operations execute in $O(1)$ constant time.

mcqs.question: Which problem is classically solved using a Stack data structure?
mcqs.explanation: Parentheses matching uses stack LIFO mechanics to pair closing brackets with most recent opening brackets.

mcqs.question: What is a 'Monotonic Stack'?
options: Stack that maintains elements strictly in increasing or decreasing order

mcqs.question: What error occurs in recursive functions when stack memory exceeds maximum call stack depth?
mcqs.explanation: Exceeding recursion call stack memory triggers Stack Overflow Error.

title: Queue
summary: FIFO structure, ENQUEUE, DEQUEUE, PEEK, Circular Queue, Deque (Double-Ended Queue), and BFS traversal.

explanation.overview: A Queue is a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) data structure where elements are added at the rear (enqueue) and removed from the front (dequeue).

sections.heading: Queue Operations & FIFO Order
sections.content:
- **Enqueue**: Adds element to rear/tail ($O(1)$).
- **Dequeue**: Removes element from front/head ($O(1)$).
- **Peek**: Inspects front element ($O(1)$).
bulletPoints: FIFO: First item enqueued is first item dequeued.
Use Cases: BFS Graph/Tree traversal, task scheduling, printer queues.

sections.heading: Deque (Double-Ended Queue)
sections.content: A **Deque** supports $O(1)$ insertions and deletions at BOTH front and rear ends. Essential for Sliding Window Maximum algorithm.
bulletPoints: Deque: Push/pop at both head and tail in $O(1)$ time.
Array Shift Warning: JS `array.shift()` is $O(N)$; use linked list or index pointers for true $O(1)$ dequeue!

keyTakeaways: Queue is FIFO (First-In, First-Out).
Core data structure used in Breadth-First Search (BFS) graph traversal.
JS `array.shift()` is $O(N)$; use double-linked list or Deque for true $O(1)$ dequeue.

mcqs.explanation: Breadth-First Search (BFS) uses a Queue to process nodes level by level.

options: `array.shift()` re-indexes all remaining N array elements, costing $O(N)$ linear time per dequeue

mcqs.question: What is a Deque (Double-Ended Queue)?
options: Data structure permitting $O(1)$ push and pop operations at BOTH front and rear ends

mcqs.explanation: Linked List based Queue operations execute in $O(1)$ constant time.

title: Linked list
summary: Singly vs Doubly Linked Lists, pointer manipulation, node insertion/deletion O(1), and list reversal.

explanation.overview: A Linked List is a linear collection of data nodes where each node contains a value and a pointer (`next` / `prev`) to adjacent nodes in memory.

sections.heading: Singly vs Doubly Linked Lists
sections.content:
- **Singly Linked List**: Each node points to `next` node.
- **Doubly Linked List**: Each node points to `next` and `prev` nodes (allows bidirectional traversal).
- **Non-Contiguous Memory**: Nodes are allocated dynamically in heap memory, connected via pointer references.
bulletPoints: Access by Index: $O(N)$ (must traverse from head node).
Insert/Delete given node pointer: $O(1)$ constant time.
No Resizing Overhead: Dynamic size without capacity reallocation.

sections.heading: Dummy Head Node Technique
sections.content: Using a `dummy` (sentinel) head node simplifies edge-case handling (inserting/deleting at head of list) by eliminating special `if (head === null)` checks.
bulletPoints: Dummy Node: `const dummy = new ListNode(0); dummy.next = head;`.
List Reversal: In-place pointer reversal in $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

keyTakeaways: Linked lists allocate non-contiguous memory connected via pointers.
Index lookup is $O(N)$; insertion/deletion at known node pointer is $O(1)$.
Use Dummy Head nodes to simplify pointer manipulation edge cases.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of inserting a new node AFTER a known node pointer reference `curr`?
mcqs.explanation: Inserting after a given node pointer reassigns `next` pointers in $O(1)$ constant time.

mcqs.explanation: Dummy head node provides a stable reference point, eliminating special null checks for list head mutations.

mcqs.explanation: Doubly Linked List nodes store 2 pointers (`next` and `prev`) per node.

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of reversing a Singly Linked List iteratively in-place?
mcqs.explanation: Iterative pointer reversal reassigns pointers in-place using $O(1)$ auxiliary space.

title: Binary search
summary: O(log N) divide and conquer search, sorted search space, overflow-safe mid calculation, and search space reduction.

explanation.overview: Binary Search is an $O(\log N)$ Divide-and-Conquer algorithm that locates a target value within a sorted search space by halving the search range at each step.

sections.heading: Binary Search Algorithm
sections.content: Maintain `left` and `right` pointers. Calculate `mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2)` (overflow-safe calculation). If `arr[mid] === target`, return index. If `arr[mid] < target`, search right half (`left = mid + 1`); else search left half (`right = mid - 1`).
bulletPoints: Sorted Prerequisite: Search space MUST be monotonic/sorted.
Overflow Prevention: Use `left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2)` instead of `(left + right) / 2` to prevent integer overflow in C++/Java.

sections.heading: Binary Search on Answer Range
sections.content: Binary Search applies beyond array indexes to continuous answer ranges (e.g. Min Capacity to Ship Packages within D Days, Koko Eating Bananas).
bulletPoints: Monotonic Search Space: Any problem where `isPossible(x)` is monotonic can be solved with Binary Search in $O(\log(\text{range}))\times O(\text{check})$ time.

keyTakeaways: Binary Search operates in $O(\log N)$ time on sorted search spaces.
Use overflow-safe mid: `mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2)`.
Apply Binary Search on Answer ranges for optimization problems.

mcqs.question: What is worst-case time complexity of Binary Search on a sorted array of N elements?
mcqs.explanation: Binary Search halves search space at each iteration step, running in $O(\log N)$ logarithmic time.

mcqs.question: Why is `mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2)` preferred over `mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2)`?
options: Prevents potential integer overflow bug when `left + right` exceeds maximum integer capacity in languages like C++/Java
mcqs.explanation: `left + (right - left) / 2` avoids potential integer overflow when `left + right` exceeds 32-bit integer limits.

mcqs.question: How many array element comparisons does Binary Search execute at most for a sorted array of 1,000,000 items?
mcqs.explanation: $\log_2(1,000,000) \approx 20$, requiring at most 20 comparisons.

mcqs.question: What condition must be satisfied to apply Binary Search to a problem?
options: Search space MUST be sorted / monotonic
mcqs.explanation: Binary Search requires a sorted/monotonic search space to determine which half to eliminate.

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of iterative Binary Search?
mcqs.explanation: Iterative Binary Search uses only a few index variables, consuming $O(1)$ space.

title: Recursion
summary: Base case vs Recursive step, Call Stack frame allocation, Stack Overflow, and Memoization.

explanation.overview: Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems until reaching a terminating Base Case.

sections.heading: Base Case & Recursive Step
sections.content:
Every recursive function requires:
1. **Base Case**: Stop condition that returns without making further recursive calls.
2. **Recursive Step**: Reduces problem size toward base case (`return n * factorial(n - 1)`).
bulletPoints: Missing Base Case: Triggers infinite recursion and Stack Overflow.
Call Stack: Each recursive call allocates a new frame on system Call Stack.

sections.heading: Memoization (Top-Down Dynamic Programming)
sections.content: Naive recursive Fibonacci `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` takes exponential $O(2^N)$ time due to overlapping redundant calls. **Memoization** caches subproblem results in a Map/Array, reducing execution time to $O(N)$ linear time.
bulletPoints: Naive Fib: $O(2^N)$ exponential explosion.
Memoized Fib: $O(N)$ linear time & $O(N)$ space.

keyTakeaways: Every recursive function MUST have a terminating Base Case.
Recursive calls consume Call Stack space ($O(H)$ space complexity).
Use Memoization to optimize recursive subproblem overlap from $O(2^N)$ to $O(N)$.

codeExamples.description: Optimizing recursive Fibonacci with memoization map.

mcqs.question: What happens if a recursive function omits a Base Case?
options: Function executes infinite recursive calls until Call Stack memory exhausts, causing a Stack Overflow Error
mcqs.explanation: Omitting a base case causes infinite recursion and Stack Overflow.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of naive un-memoized recursive Fibonacci `fib(N) = fib(N-1) + fib(N-2)`?
mcqs.explanation: Naive recursive Fibonacci generates binary recursion tree of depth N, taking $O(2^N)$ exponential time.

mcqs.question: How does Memoization optimize recursive algorithms with overlapping subproblems?
options: Caches subproblem results in a Map/Array, avoiding duplicate recalculation of solved subproblems
mcqs.explanation: Memoization stores subproblem solutions, reducing exponential calls to linear $O(N)$.

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of a recursive function that recurses to maximum depth $H$?
mcqs.explanation: The Call Stack retains $H$ frame pointers at maximum recursion depth ($O(H)$ space).

mcqs.question: What is Tail Call Optimization (TCO)?
options: Compiler optimization where recursive call is final statement in function, allowing engine to reuse stack frame without growing stack
mcqs.explanation: Tail Call Optimization reuses current stack frame for tail-recursive calls, avoiding stack growth.

title: Trees
summary: Binary Trees, Binary Search Trees (BST), AVL/Red-Black balanced trees, tree traversals (In-order, Pre-order, Post-order).

explanation.overview: A Tree is a hierarchical non-linear data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges, starting from a single Root node.

sections.heading: Binary Search Tree (BST) Property
sections.content:
In a **Binary Search Tree (BST)**, for every node:
- All values in `left` subtree are strictly LESS than node value.
- All values in `right` subtree are strictly GREATER than node value.
bulletPoints: Balanced BST Operations: Search, Insert, Delete run in $O(\log N)$ time.
Unbalanced Degenerate BST: Degenerates to linked list ($O(N)$ operations).
Self-Balancing Trees: AVL Trees and Red-Black Trees rebalance automatically to maintain $O(\log N)$ depth.

sections.heading: Depth-First Tree Traversals
sections.content:
1. **In-Order** (Left, Root, Right): Yields elements in **sorted ascending order** for BST!
2. **Pre-Order** (Root, Left, Right): Useful for tree cloning/serialization.
3. **Post-Order** (Left, Right, Root): Useful for tree deletion / bottom-up calculations.
bulletPoints: In-Order BST: Always visits nodes in sorted order.
Pre-Order: Root processed first.
Post-Order: Children processed before root.

keyTakeaways: BST property: Left < Root < Right.
In-Order traversal on BST visits nodes in sorted ascending order.
Balanced BSTs achieve $O(\log N)$ search/insert/delete speed.

codeExamples.description: Recursive In-Order traversal yielding sorted values.

mcqs.question: Which tree traversal order visits nodes of a Binary Search Tree (BST) in **sorted ascending order**?
mcqs.explanation: In-Order traversal (Left, Root, Right) visits BST nodes in sorted order.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of searching for a value in a Balanced Binary Search Tree (BST) of N nodes?
mcqs.explanation: Balanced BSTs halve search space at each step, running in $O(\log N)$ logarithmic time.

mcqs.question: What is worst-case time complexity of searching an Unbalanced Degenerate BST (e.g., nodes inserted in sorted order 1, 2, 3, 4)?
options: O(N) linear time (degenerates to linked list)
mcqs.explanation: An unbalanced BST degenerates into a linear linked list ($O(N)$ depth).

mcqs.question: Which traversal order processes Root node BEFORE visiting left and right child subtrees?
mcqs.explanation: Pre-Order traversal processes Root first, then Left and Right subtrees.

mcqs.question: What self-balancing Binary Search Tree structure is used by C++ `std::map` and Java `TreeMap`?
mcqs.explanation: Red-Black Trees are self-balancing BSTs used by C++ `std::map` and Java `TreeMap`.

title: BFS
summary: Breadth-First Search, Queue-based level-order traversal, unweighted shortest path, O(V + E) complexity.

explanation.overview: Breadth-First Search (BFS) is an algorithm for searching tree or graph data structures level-by-level using a **Queue**.

sections.heading: BFS Algorithm & Queue Mechanics
sections.content:
Algorithm steps:
1. Initialize Queue with start node; mark node as visited.
2. While Queue is not empty, dequeue current node.
3. Process node and enqueue all unvisited neighbor nodes.
bulletPoints: Data Structure: Uses **Queue** (FIFO) data structure.
Visited Set: Track visited nodes to prevent infinite loops in graphs with cycles.
Time Complexity: $O(V + E)$ where $V$ = Vertices, $E$ = Edges.

sections.heading: Shortest Path Guarantee in Unweighted Graphs
sections.content: BFS guarantees finding the **shortest path** (fewest number of edges) from source node to target node in unweighted graphs.
bulletPoints: Unweighted Shortest Path: First time target node is dequeued represents shortest distance.
Level-Order Traversal: Processes nodes at distance $d$ before distance $d+1$.

keyTakeaways: BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) for level-by-level traversal.
Guarantees finding shortest path in unweighted graphs.
Time complexity: $O(V + E)$; Space complexity: $O(V)$ for Queue & Visited set.

codeExamples.title: BFS Tree Level-Order Traversal
codeExamples.description: Level-order traversal of Binary Tree using Queue.

mcqs.question: Which data structure is required to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
mcqs.explanation: BFS requires a Queue (FIFO) to explore nodes level-by-level.

mcqs.question: What shortest path guarantee does BFS provide?
options: Guarantees shortest path in weighted graphs
Guarantees shortest path (fewest edges) in UNWEIGHTED graphs
mcqs.explanation: BFS guarantees finding shortest path (fewest edge hops) in unweighted graphs.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of BFS traversal on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
mcqs.explanation: BFS visits every vertex $V$ and traverses every edge $E$ once ($O(V + E)$).

mcqs.question: Why is a `Visited` set required during BFS graph traversal?
options: Prevents infinite loops by avoiding re-visiting already processed graph nodes in cyclic graphs
mcqs.explanation: A Visited set tracks explored nodes, preventing infinite loops in cyclic graphs.

mcqs.question: What is worst-case space complexity of BFS on a tree with maximum breadth B?
options: O(B) matching maximum width/level size of tree
mcqs.explanation: BFS Queue stores all nodes present in widest tree level ($O(B)$ space).

title: DFS
summary: Depth-First Search, Stack/Recursion implementation, connected components, cycle detection, and Backtracking.

explanation.overview: Depth-First Search (DFS) is an algorithm for traversing trees or graphs by exploring as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.

sections.heading: DFS Algorithm Mechanics
sections.content: Uses **Call Stack (Recursion)** or explicit LIFO Stack. Visits node, marks visited, and recursively explores first unvisited neighbor until reaching leaf/dead end, then backtracks.
bulletPoints: Data Structure: **Call Stack / Recursion** or explicit Stack.
Deep Exploration: Plunges deep into branch before backtracking.
Time Complexity: $O(V + E)$.

sections.heading: DFS Use Cases & Backtracking
sections.content:
- **Connected Components**: Count island grids (Number of Islands).
- **Cycle Detection**: Detect cycles in directed graphs (three-color marking).
- **Backtracking**: Generate permutations, combinations, and solve Sudoku/N-Queens.
bulletPoints: Backtracking: Undo choices (`visited.delete(node)`) when returning from recursion.
Topological Sort: Post-order DFS sorting for DAG task scheduling.

keyTakeaways: DFS uses Recursion / Call Stack to explore deep branches.
Primary tool for Backtracking (permutations, N-Queens) and island counting.
Time complexity: $O(V + E)$; Space complexity: $O(H)$ matching maximum call stack depth.

codeExamples.title: DFS Grid Traversal (Number of Islands)
codeExamples.description: Counting connected island components using recursive DFS.

mcqs.question: Which underlying mechanism powers recursive Depth-First Search (DFS)?
mcqs.explanation: Recursive DFS utilizes the system Call Stack to manage call frames.

mcqs.question: What is primary difference in search pattern between DFS and BFS?
options: DFS explores as deep as possible down a single branch before backtracking; BFS explores level-by-level outwards
mcqs.explanation: DFS explores deeply along a single path before backtracking; BFS explores level-by-level.

mcqs.question: What technique extends DFS to solve combinatorial search problems (N-Queens, Sudoku) by undoing choices upon returning from recursive calls?
mcqs.explanation: Backtracking uses DFS recursion, undoing choices when returning from dead ends.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
mcqs.explanation: DFS visits every vertex $V$ and traverses every edge $E$ once ($O(V + E)$).

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of recursive DFS on a tree of height $H$?
mcqs.explanation: Recursive DFS call stack space matches maximum tree height depth ($O(H)$).

title: Sorting
summary: Comparison sorting algorithms: QuickSort, Merge Sort, HeapSort, Bubble/Selection/Insertion sort, stability, and space/time tradeoffs.

explanation.overview: Sorting rearranges elements of an array in a specific order (ascending or descending).

sections.heading: Common Sorting Algorithms Comparison
sections.content:
- **Merge Sort**: Divide and Conquer. Guaranteed $O(N \log N)$ time, $O(N)$ space. **Stable**.
- **QuickSort**: Divide and Conquer (Pivot partitioning). Average $O(N \log N)$ time, $O(1)$ space. Worst-case $O(N^2)$ if pivot choice is bad. **Unstable**.
- **HeapSort**: Uses Max-Heap. $O(N \log N)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Unstable**.
- **Bubble / Insertion / Selection Sort**: Simple $O(N^2)$ quadratic algorithms.
bulletPoints: Merge Sort: Stable $O(N \log N)$ time, $O(N)$ space.
QuickSort: Average $O(N \log N)$ time, $O(1)$ space.
Stability: Preserves relative order of equal elements.

sections.heading: Stable vs Unstable Sorting
sections.content: A sorting algorithm is **Stable** if it maintains relative original order of items with identical key values.
bulletPoints: Stable Sorts: Merge Sort, Insertion Sort, Timsort.
Unstable Sorts: QuickSort, HeapSort, Selection Sort.

keyTakeaways: Merge Sort guarantees $O(N \log N)$ time and stability ($O(N)$ space).
QuickSort provides average $O(N \log N)$ time with $O(1)$ in-place space.
Stable sorting preserves relative original order of equal elements.

codeExamples.description: Recursive Divide and Conquer Merge Sort algorithm.

mcqs.question: What is WORST-CASE time complexity of QuickSort if pivot choice is consistently worst element?
mcqs.explanation: Bad pivot selection (e.g. sorted array with first element pivot) degrades QuickSort to $O(N^2)$ quadratic time.

mcqs.question: Which sorting algorithm guarantees $O(N \log N)$ worst-case time complexity AND is Stable?
mcqs.explanation: Merge Sort guarantees $O(N \log N)$ time in worst case and is a Stable sorting algorithm.

mcqs.question: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be 'Stable'?
options: Preserves relative original order of elements with equal key values
mcqs.explanation: Stable sorting maintains relative input sequence order for elements with equal values.

mcqs.question: What hybrid sorting algorithm is used by JavaScript `Array.prototype.sort()` and Python `sort()`?
mcqs.explanation: Timsort is hybrid stable sorting algorithm used in V8 JS and Python.

mcqs.question: What is lower bound theoretical time complexity limit for any comparison-based sorting algorithm?
mcqs.explanation: Comparison-based sorting has a mathematical lower bound of $\Omega(N \log N)$ operations.

title: Heap
summary: Binary Heap complete tree, Min-Heap vs Max-Heap, array representation, insertion/extract O(log N), Priority Queue.

explanation.overview: A Binary Heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the Heap Property, serving as efficient implementation for Priority Queues.

sections.heading: Min-Heap vs Max-Heap Property
sections.content:
- **Min-Heap**: Value of parent node is $\le$ values of its children (root holds MINIMUM element).
- **Max-Heap**: Value of parent node is $\ge$ values of its children (root holds MAXIMUM element).
bulletPoints: Min-Heap Root: Always stores minimum element.
Max-Heap Root: Always stores maximum element.
Peek Top: $O(1)$ constant time access to min/max.

sections.heading: Array Representation & Time Complexities
sections.content:
Heaps are stored in compact zero-indexed arrays without pointers:
- Left Child: `2 * i + 1`
- Right Child: `2 * i + 2`
- Parent: `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`
Operations: `insert` $O(\log N)$, `extractMin/Max` $O(\log N)$, `peek` $O(1)$, `heapify` array $O(N)$.
bulletPoints: Insert (Bubble Up): $O(\log N)$ time.
Extract Top (Bubble Down): $O(\log N)$ time.
Build Heap (Heapify): $O(N)$ linear time.

keyTakeaways: Min-Heap root holds smallest element; Max-Heap root holds largest.
Operations: `peek` $O(1)$, `insert`/`extract` $O(\log N)$, `heapify` $O(N)$.
Power Priority Queues and Top-K Frequent Element algorithms.

codeExamples.description: Min-Heap array representation with bubbleUp and bubbleDown.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of peeking minimum element `peek()` at root of a Min-Heap?
mcqs.explanation: Min-Heap root node holds minimum element, accessible in $O(1)$ constant time.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of `insert()` or `extractMin()` operations on a Heap of N items?
mcqs.explanation: Bubbling up or sifting down along heap height depth executes in $O(\log N)$ time.

mcqs.question: In 0-indexed array representation of a Binary Heap, what index formula calculates Left Child of parent index `i`?
mcqs.explanation: In 0-indexed array heaps, Left Child is located at index `2 * i + 1`.

mcqs.question: What is time complexity of converting an unsorted array of N elements into a Heap using `heapify` (Floyd's algorithm)?
mcqs.explanation: Floyd's bottom-up `heapify` algorithm builds a Heap from array in $O(N)$ linear time.

mcqs.question: Which algorithm pattern uses a Min-Heap of size K to find K Largest Elements in an array of N items in $O(N \log K)$ time?
mcqs.explanation: Maintaining a Min-Heap of size K solves Top-K Largest Elements in $O(N \log K)$ time.

title: Basic graphs
summary: Directed vs Undirected graphs, Adjacency List vs Adjacency Matrix, weighted edges, and graph representations.

explanation.overview: A Graph is a non-linear network data structure consisting of a set of Vertices (Nodes, $V$) connected by Edges ($E$).

sections.heading: Directed vs Undirected & Weighted Graphs
sections.content:
- **Undirected Graph**: Edges are bidirectional (`A <-> B`).
- **Directed Graph (DAG)**: Edges have direction (`A -> B`).
- **Weighted Graph**: Edges carry numerical weight cost values.
bulletPoints: Undirected: Symmetry in edge connections.
Directed (DAG): Directed Acyclic Graph used in task scheduling.
Weighted: Edges carry distance/cost values (Dijkstra's algorithm).

sections.heading: Adjacency List vs Adjacency Matrix
sections.content:
- **Adjacency List**: Hash Map/Array of lists (`Map<Node, Node[]>`). Space complexity $O(V + E)$. Ideal for sparse graphs.
- **Adjacency Matrix**: 2D boolean array $V \times V$. Space complexity $O(V^2)$. Ideal for dense graphs.
bulletPoints: Adjacency List: $O(V + E)$ space (sparse graphs).
Adjacency Matrix: $O(V^2)$ space (instant $O(1)$ edge existence check).

keyTakeaways: Adjacency Lists use $O(V + E)$ space (standard for sparse graphs).
Adjacency Matrices use $O(V^2)$ space.
Use Adjacency Lists for BFS and DFS graph traversals.

codeExamples.description: Building undirected graph Adjacency List in JavaScript.

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of an Adjacency List representation of a graph with V vertices and E edges?
mcqs.explanation: Adjacency List stores $V$ vertex entries and $E$ edge references ($O(V + E)$ space).

mcqs.question: What is space complexity of an Adjacency Matrix 2D grid representation for a graph of V vertices?
mcqs.explanation: Adjacency Matrix allocates a 2D $V \times V$ grid ($O(V^2)$ space).

mcqs.question: Which graph representation allows checking if edge exists between node A and node B in $O(1)$ constant time?
mcqs.explanation: Adjacency Matrix cell `matrix[A][B]` direct lookup executes in $O(1)$ constant time.

mcqs.question: What is a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)?
options: A directed graph containing NO directed cycles
mcqs.explanation: DAG is a directed graph containing zero directed cycles, enabling Topological Sorting.

mcqs.question: Which graph representation is best suited for sparse graphs where edge count E is far smaller than $V^2$?
mcqs.explanation: Adjacency Lists save massive RAM on sparse graphs by storing only actual existing edges.
